This section relaxes the assumption (S), then the assumption that every central city is joined to
$C_I$ and $C_G$. It corresponds to §6 of the
[theory note](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/master/doc/theory/exact-front.md).

## Non-Symmetric Clique MultiZenoTravel {#sec-nonsym}

In this section, we relax the Assumption (S). As a result, the previous method does not work in
the particular case a $(B\bar B)$-pairing is not possible. More precisely, it happens when there
is no choice of cities to perform a $(B\bar B)$-pairing because for two cities $C_i$ and $C_j$
(resp. for $B$ and $\bar B$) we have $d_i < d_j$ and $\bar d_j < \bar d_i$. In such case, the
$(B\bar B)$-pairing on $C_i$ (resp. $C_j$) would increase the duration of the pattern $\bar B$
(resp. $B$) by $2(\bar d_i - \bar d_j)$ (resp. $2(d_j - d_i)$). As a result, without any other
change, the transformed plan has a larger total flight duration for at least one plane which may
result in a larger makespan.

Two regimes must be distinguished. When no flight between central cities is shorter than a detour
through $C_I$ or $C_G$, assumption (A1-NS), the method carries over with durations that depend on
the role of each landing, provided the makespan accounts for the waiting it may force. When such
flights are shorter, plans that move passengers between central cities, the $B\bar A\bar B$
situations among them, can beat every plan of $2t - p$ simple patterns.

### Role configurations {#sec-roles}

A pattern $A$ or $\bar A$ in $C_w$ lasts $d_w + \bar d_w$, a pattern $B$ lasts $2 d_w$ and a
pattern $\bar B$ lasts $2\bar d_w$. Lists of cities are therefore replaced by role configurations
({{< node "Definition 4.2" >}}): for each plane $k$, the cities of its patterns $B$
($\mathrm{Dr}_k$), $\bar B$ ($\mathrm{Pk}_k$) and $A$ or $\bar A$ ($\mathrm{Cr}_k$), balanced city
by city, with the role load
$\lambda_k = 2\delta(\mathrm{Dr}_k) + 2\bar\delta(\mathrm{Pk}_k) + \delta(\mathrm{Cr}_k) + \bar\delta(\mathrm{Cr}_k)$.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 6.1" >}} **Converse to role configurations.** Assume (A1-NS). For every
feasible plan with cost $C$ and makespan $M$ there is a role configuration on the $p$ planes with
passenger count $t$, cost at most $C$ and $\lambda_k \le F_k \le M$ for every $k$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Replace each flight $a \to b$ between central cities by $a \to h \to b$ through the hub
$h$ for which the detour is no longer, which exists by (A1-NS); clean the journeys, and apply the
direct selection and shrinking lemmas ({{< node "Lemma 4.3" badge=false >}},
{{< node "Lemma 4.4" badge=false >}}; {{< node "Theorem 6.1" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

Without (A1-NS), {{< node "Lemma 6.2" >}} still gives a lower bound $L_{\rm NS}$ under (AΔ), by
requiring the balance only in total rather than city by city, whatever the flights between central
cities. The least cost $E_{\rm NS}(T)$ of a role configuration with every $\lambda_k \le T$ is the
shortest path of a dynamic program over *imbalance vectors*, the per-city difference between
patterns $B$ and $\bar B$ so far ({{< node "Proposition 6.6" >}}); it is polynomial in $n$ and
$2t - p$ for fixed $t - p$.

### Waiting {#sec-waiting}

If a non-symmetric instance is highly imbalanced in durations, while performing a
$(B\bar B)$-pairing, there is a chance that the plane performing $\bar B$ will have to wait. It
implies that its makespan is not the sum of the durations of its patterns but the moment the
passenger arrives in the central city, plus the remaining duration of its sequence.

Fix an order of the patterns $B$ and of the patterns $\bar B$ of every plane, and a *link
matching*: in each city, which pattern $B$ feeds which pattern $\bar B$. The *template* flies
every plane's patterns $B$ in order from time 0, then its patterns $A$ and $\bar A$, then its
patterns $\bar B$ in order, every flight departing as soon as possible, a pattern $\bar B$ leaving
its city only once its passenger is there. Let
$\mathrm{Pre}_u(j) = 2\sum_{j' < j} d_{\mathrm{Dr}_u[j']}$ be the duration of the patterns $B$
that plane $u$ flies before its $j$-th, and
$\mathrm{Suf}_v(l) = 2\sum_{l' > l} \bar d_{\mathrm{Pk}_v[l']}$ that of the patterns $\bar B$ that
plane $v$ flies after its $l$-th.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 6.3" >}} **Template.** The template is a plan, and its makespan is
$$M_{\rm tmpl} = \max\Big(\max_k \lambda_k,\ \max_{(u, j;\, v, l) \text{ linked in } C_i}\ \mathrm{Pre}_u(j) + d_i + \bar d_i + \mathrm{Suf}_v(l)\Big).$$
Every plan that flies the same configuration with the same orders and matching has makespan at
least $M_{\rm tmpl}$. The *least makespan* of the configuration is the minimum of $M_{\rm tmpl}$
over orders and matchings.
:::

A link term is the length of a chain that no plan can shorten: the plane performing $B$ flies its
earlier patterns $B$ and reaches $C_i$, the passenger then needs $\bar d_i$ to reach $C_G$, and the
plane performing $\bar B$ still flies its later patterns $\bar B$. With a single pattern $\bar B$
per plane, as in the construction of Theorem 4.1, the chain never exceeds the loads:

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Corollary 6.4" >}} **One pick-up never waits harmfully.** Assume (AΔ-path). If every
plane performs at most one pattern $\bar B$, then $M_{\rm tmpl} = \max_k \lambda_k$ for every
order and matching. The same holds if every plane performs at most one pattern $B$.
:::

One may hope that waiting can always be avoided by choosing the orders and the matching well, so
that the Pareto front would be the Pareto set of (cost, largest role load) over role
configurations. This is Conjecture 6.5, and it is false.

::: {.statement .refuted}
{{< node "Conjecture 6.5" >}} **No harmful waiting.** Under (AΔ-path), every role configuration
has orders and a matching with $M_{\rm tmpl} = \max_k \lambda_k$; in a weaker form, the Pareto
front is the Pareto set of (cost, $\max_k \lambda_k$) over role configurations.
:::

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 6.5" >}} **Harmful waiting.** Take $n = 2$ cities with $d = (3, 19)$,
$\bar d = (3, 11)$, $c = (5, 1)$, $t = 7$ passengers, $p = 4$ planes and no flight between
central cities. The cheapest role configuration with every $\lambda_k \le 73$ costs 14, but no
plan of makespan at most 73 costs less than 18.
:::

A configuration has $2t - p = 10$ landings, so cost 14 means one landing in $C_1$ and nine in
$C_2$. A pattern $A$ or $\bar A$ weighs 6 in $C_1$ and 30 in $C_2$, a $B$ 6 and 38, a $\bar B$ 6 and
22, which leaves one shape within 73: three planes perform an $A$ and a $B$ in $C_2$ (load 68),
and the fourth plane $v$ an $A$ in $C_1$ and the three patterns $\bar B$ in $C_2$ (load
$6 + 3 \cdot 22 = 72$). Every passenger left in $C_2$ arrives there at time 19 or later, but $v$
reaches $C_2$ for its first $\bar B$ at $6 + 11 = 17$. It waits until 19, and its two other
patterns $\bar B$ take 44 more: it finishes at $74 > 72$. The whole front was computed, by an
oracle over role-configuration schedules, by the solver and by an exhaustive search over all
plans (937 million states, plans with extra landings included):
$$(10, 90),\ (14, 74),\ (18, 68),\ (22, 66),\ (26, 52),\ (34, 42),\ (38, 36),\ (42, 30),\ (50, 18),$$
while ignoring waiting would add $(14, 72)$ and $(30, 50)$ (@fig-waiting).

![The instance of Proposition 6.5 (experiment E5). Left: the Pareto front with exact waiting (blue) and the two points that only exist when waiting is ignored (orange). Right: the share of random instances on which waiting changes the front, for uniform durations and for instances shaped like Proposition 6.5, with 95% Wilson intervals.](figures/e5-harmful_waiting.svg){#fig-waiting .paper-fig}

Harmful waiting needs a plane with several patterns $\bar B$ in a city $C_y$ whose first one
arrives before the earliest passenger left there, that is, a short phase of patterns $A$ and
$\bar A$ with $d_x + \bar d_x + \bar d_y < d_y$ for its crossing city $x$. (AΔ-path) bounds
$\bar d$ by $d$ but not $d$ by $\bar d$, so it does not prevent this. It is rare: in the experiment
[E5](experiments.qmd#sec-e5), random configurations waited harmfully at most 29 times in a million
draws, and waiting changed the front of 9 of 150 instances shaped like Proposition 6.5 and of none
of 150 uniform ones.

### The non-symmetric Pareto front {#sec-ns-front}

Theorem 6.1 bounds the role loads of the configuration it selects, but not its waiting, since it
pairs patterns $B$ and $\bar B$ by counts per city and not along the plan's own hand-offs. The
following theorem selects the pairings along the hand-offs, after removing those that the planes
could have avoided. Plans with zero durations need care: {{< node "Lemma 6.8" >}} shows that a plan
fails to be event-ordered exactly when the relation "next flight on the plane or on the journey"
has a cycle, that such a cycle passes through a city with $d_x = \bar d_x = 0$, and that templates
and the plans of Theorem 4.1 are event-ordered.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 6.9" >}} **Schedulable domination.** Assume (A1-NS). For every feasible plan
with cost $C$ and makespan $M$, there are a role configuration on the $p$ planes with passenger
count $t$ and cost at most $C$, orders of its patterns $B$ and $\bar B$, and a link matching whose
template has makespan at most $M$. Neither an event order, nor (AΔ), nor (AΔ-path) is needed.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Make the plan simple and clean, then rewire hand-offs by three moves (an *exchange* of
the rest of the sequences of two planes that meet, a *cut* of a zero-time detour into a separate
loop, and a *splice* of such a loop back into a sequence), each of which carries one more passenger
through a single pattern, until every remaining hand-off goes forward in time. The hand-offs then
form chains from a pattern $B$ to a pattern $\bar B$, which give the links, and along each chain
the link term of Lemma 6.3 is at most $M$ ({{< node "Theorem 6.9" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Corollary 6.10" >}} **Non-symmetric front.** Assume (A1-NS). Let $\mathcal K$ be the
set of pairs (cost, least makespan) of the role configurations on the $p$ planes with passenger
count $t$, and $\mathcal A_{\rm eo}$ the set of points of feasible event-ordered plans. Then
$\mathcal F = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal A_{\rm eo} = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal K$.
:::

So under (A1-NS) a constructive algorithm can still focus on plans with $2t - p$ central cities,
with additional care for waiting. ZenoSolver brackets every level between the lower bounds
$L_{\rm NS}$ and $E_{\rm NS}$ and the templates of the configurations it builds, which never wait
when each plane performs at most one $\bar B$ (Corollary 6.4). A gap between consecutive achieved
points $(C_i, M_i)$ and $(C_{i+1}, M_{i+1})$ is closed by enumerating the configurations of cost
below $C_i$ whose loads are at most $M_{i+1} - 1$, and computing the least makespan of each by a
search over orders and matchings with the closed form of Lemma 6.3. Proposition 6.5 shows that the
search can be needed. The experiment [E4](experiments.qmd#sec-e4) compares the resulting fronts
with exhaustive searches over all plans.

### BĀB̄ situations {#sec-short}

Without (A1-NS), a flight between central cities can be shorter than any detour through $C_I$ or
$C_G$, and plans of simple patterns can miss the Pareto front: a first search found 11 such
instances among 140. The natural candidates for the missing plans are the patterns with one flight
between central cities.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Definition 6.17" >}} **Shuttle triple, split crossing.** Let $C_x \ne C_y$ be central
cities joined by a flight. A *shuttle* from $C_x$ to $C_y$ is a pattern $C_G \to C_x \to C_y \to C_I$
(type $\bar A$) that carries a passenger from $C_x$ to $C_y$. A $B\bar A\bar B$ *situation*, or
*shuttle triple*, is a pattern $B$ in $C_x$, a shuttle from $C_x$ to $C_y$ and a pattern $\bar B$
in $C_y$, carrying one passenger. A *split crossing* is a pattern $C_I \to C_x \to C_y \to C_G$
(type $A$) whose flight between central cities is empty: its first flight leaves a passenger in
$C_x$, and its last flight carries another one from $C_y$ to $C_G$.
:::

A shuttle and a split crossing fly the same three flights in opposite directions, but a split
crossing is an $A$, while a shuttle is an $\bar A$, whose plane needs two more patterns $A$
({{< node "Lemma 2.1" badge=false >}}). One may hope that $B\bar A\bar B$ situations complete the
front, as in the following conjecture. They do not.

::: {.statement .refuted}
{{< node "Conjecture 6.7" >}} **Shuttle triples complete the front.** Under (AΔ), the Pareto front
is the Pareto set of (cost, least makespan) over role configurations extended with $B\bar A\bar B$
situations.
:::

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 6.7" >}} **Shuttles are not enough.** Take $n = 2$, $d = (1, 3)$,
$\bar d = (3, 1)$, $d_{12} = 2$, $t = 3$, $p = 2$ and any costs. (AΔ) holds and (A1-NS) fails.
Some plan has makespan 8, but every plan whose flights between central cities all lie in patterns
$\bar A$ has makespan at least 10. With $c = (6, 1)$ the Pareto front is
$\{(4, 10), (15, 8)\}$, and plans with shuttles only, like role configurations, give
$\{(4, 10)\}$.
:::

::: {#fig-split}

The plan of makespan 8 of Proposition 6.7 ($I = C_I$, $G = C_G$; dashed flights are empty).
$p_2$ performs the split crossing $C_I \to C_2 \to C_1 \to C_G$: it leaves $t_3$ in $C_2$ at time 3,
flies empty to $C_1$, and carries $t_1$, left there by $p_1$ at time 1, to $C_G$. $p_1$ takes $t_3$
from $C_2$ at time 7. Both planes finish at 8; the landings are $C_1, C_2, C_2$ and $C_2, C_1$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch of the bound.* A pattern $A$ or $\bar A$ lasts at least $\min_x(d_x + \bar d_x) = 4$, and a
plane with an $\bar A$ performs at least three such patterns, so a plan of makespan below 12 whose
flights between central cities lie in patterns $\bar A$ has none. On the instance without that
flight, Theorem 6.1 gives a role configuration with every load at most the makespan, and a case
check on its four landings shows that some load is at least 10
({{< node "Proposition 6.7" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

This is the case of the beginning of this section: $d_1 < d_2$ and $\bar d_2 < \bar d_1$, so no
$(B\bar B)$-pairing within one city is short, as one costs $2 d_x + 2\bar d_x = 8$ in either city.
The split crossing enters at $C_2$, next to $C_G$, and leaves from $C_1$, next to $C_I$; it lets
$p_1$ leave a passenger in $C_1$ and take another from $C_2$ for 2 each, a pairing between two
different cities. Split crossings do not complete the front either:

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 6.18" >}} **One flight between central cities per pattern is not enough.**
In each instance below, (AΔ) holds and (A1-NS) fails.

*(a)* $n = 2$, $d = (1, 7)$, $\bar d = (7, 1)$, $d_{12} = 6$ (the least value (AΔ) allows),
$t = 5$, $p = 2$, any costs. The least makespan of a plan is 32, reached with the pattern
$C_I \to C_2 \to C_1 \to C_2 \to C_1 \to C_G$. Plans whose patterns each make at most three central
landings need 34, and role configurations 36.

*(b)* $n = 3$, $d = (1, 3, 2)$, $\bar d = (3, 1, 2)$, flights $C_1$–$C_3$ and $C_2$–$C_3$ of
duration 1 and none between $C_1$ and $C_2$, $c = (0, 0, 1)$, $t = 3$, $p = 2$. The Pareto front is
$\{(0, 10), (1, 8)\}$; plans whose patterns make at most two central landings give
$\{(0, 10), (2, 8)\}$. The point $(1, 8)$ needs the split crossing routed through $C_3$,
$C_I \to C_2 \to C_3 \to C_1 \to C_G$.

*(c)* $n = 2$, $d = (3, 8)$, $\bar d = (8, 3)$, $d_{12} = 5$, $t = 7$, $p = 3$. The least makespan,
41, needs a pattern that lands six times; with at most five central landings per pattern it is 43.

*(d)* $n = 3$, $d = (7, 1, 3)$, $\bar d = (2, 6, 6)$, $c = (4, 7, 4)$, $d_{12} = 7$, $d_{13} = 5$,
$d_{23} = 3$, $t = 7$, $p = 3$. The point $(73, 29)$ is on the front, reached by a plan with the
pattern $\bar B$: $C_G \to C_3 \to C_1 \to C_3 \to C_G$, and no plan whose flights between central
cities all lie in patterns $A$ reaches makespan 29.
:::

Parts (a) to (c) were established by exhaustive search over the plans of each class of patterns,
and cross-checked with an integer flow model (computed). For (d), the exhaustive search gives the
plan and the front point, but the claim about patterns $A$ rests on the flow model alone, whose
exactness for a class of patterns has no written proof; that claim is a sketch. The searches found
no instance that needs more than six central landings in a pattern.

One lower bound holds for every plan, with no assumption at all.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 6.19" >}} **Cut bound.** Let $\Phi$ be the least flight time of a sequence of
flights from $C_I$ to $C_G$. Every feasible plan has $\sum_k F_k \ge (2t - p)\Phi$, so its makespan
is at least $(2t - p)\Phi/p$. Under (AΔ), $\Phi = \min_x(d_x + \bar d_x)$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* With $\phi(v)$ the least flight time from $C_I$ to $v$, each journey climbs at least
$\Phi$ in $\phi$, journeys use distinct flights, and each plane climbs exactly $\Phi$ more than it
descends; adding up gives $\sum_k F_k \ge 2t\Phi - p\Phi$
({{< node "Lemma 6.19" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

In Proposition 6.7 and in 6.18(a) and (c), the least makespan of all plans is this bound rounded
up (8, 32 and 41), while role configurations stay above it. For clique instances without (A1-NS),
$L_{\rm NS}$ and the cut bound are lower bounds, plans built from role configurations and from the
patterns above are upper bounds, and exact fronts come from exhaustive search or the flow model on
small instances. In the searches, shuttles never improved a front, split crossings completed it
on all but 2 of 600 random instances, and on 150 instances whose durations $d$ and $\bar d$ order
the cities alike, flights between central cities never changed it. A combinatorial description of
the front is open ([perspectives](conclusion.qmd#sec-open)).

## General MultiZenoTravel {#sec-graphs}

We now consider a connected weighted graph $U = (V, E)$ such that $|V| = n + 2$ and two arbitrary
vertices named $I$ and $G$ (with weight 0), respectively for the initial and the goal cities, not
joined by an edge. A MultiZenoTravel instance $\Pi$ is defined by the triplet $(U, I, G)$; its
plans are those of the [model](model.qmd#sec-plans), with the edges of $U$ as flights. We denote
by $\Lambda$ the set of paths over $U$, and for any path $q$, $|q|$ is the number of cities in the
path. We define the functions $\phi$ (resp. $\omega$) as follows:
$$\phi(q) = \sum_{0 \le i < |q| - 1} \mathrm{dur}(q_i, q_{i+1}), \qquad \omega(q) = \sum_{1 \le i < |q|} c_{q_i}.$$
The function $\phi$ provides the duration, while $\omega$ provides the landing cost of the path.
Notice that the first city in a path does not appear in $\omega$ because the initial state is such
that the planes are in the initial city.

The following algorithm $f$ transforms the general MultiZenoTravel transport problem defined by
$(U, I, G)$ into a non-symmetric clique problem:

* For each vertex $i$ find all the simple paths from $I$ to $i$ (resp. from $i$ to $G$) and
  denote this set $\Lambda_{I \to i}$ (resp. $\Lambda_{i \to G}$).
* Construct a new clique instance such that for each
  $(w_i, e_i) \in \Lambda_{I \to i} \times \Lambda_{i \to G}$, there is a city of weight
  $\omega(w_i) + \omega(e_i)$ (the cost of landing in $C_i$ is counted only once) and an edge
  $I \to i$ (resp. $i \to G$) of weight $\phi(w_i)$ (resp. $\phi(e_i)$).
* For all couples of cities $(i, j)$ of the new instance, assign $d_{ij} = +\infty$.

The reduced instance has no flight between central cities, so it satisfies (A1-NS), and its
Pareto front is computed as above. Every city of $f(U)$ stands for one way of reaching a central
vertex and one way of leaving it, and a pattern of $f(U)$ visits one city. A pattern of $U$, from
$I$ or $G$ to $I$ or $G$, may visit several central vertices and hand passengers over at any of
them. The reduction is therefore exact in one direction only.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 6.12" >}} **A solution to the transformed problem is a solution to the
generic problem.** For every role configuration of $f(U)$, every order and every link matching,
$U$ has a feasible plan with the configuration's cost and the makespan of its template. Hence
$\mathcal F_{f(U)} \subseteq \mathcal A_U$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Fly the template of $f(U)$ in $U$, each flight between a hub and a city $(w, e)$ being
replaced by the path it stands for. A single pattern $B$ or $\bar B$ is charged differently in
$U$ and in $f(U)$, but the two patterns of a $(B\bar B)$-pairing in one city cost together what
$f$ charges for them ({{< node "Proposition 6.12" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

{{< node "Proposition 6.13" >}} adds that $U$ and $f(U)$ have the same least cost: with
$\kappa^\star$ the least landing cost of a path from $I$ to $G$, every plan of $U$ costs at least
$(2t - p)\kappa^\star$, and the cheapest point of $\mathcal F_{f(U)}$ costs exactly that. The
converse inclusion fails, already on a path.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Example 6.11" >}} **The reduction misses the front.** Let $U$ be the path
$C_I, a, b, C_G$ with durations $1, 2, 1$ and $c_a = c_b = 1$, with $t = 3$ and $p = 2$. Then
$f(U)$ has two cities, with $(d, \bar d, c) = (1, 3, 2)$ and $(3, 1, 2)$, and
$$\mathcal F_{f(U)} = \{(8, 10)\}, \qquad \mathcal F_U = \{(8, 8)\}.$$
:::

::: {#fig-path}

A plan of cost 8 and makespan 8 on the path of Example 6.11 ($I = C_I$, $G = C_G$; dashed flights
are empty). $p_1$ leaves $t_2$ in $b$ at time 3, flies back to $a$, and takes $t_3$ from there at
time 5, all within the single pattern $C_I\,a\,b\,a\,b\,C_G$. Each plane lands twice in $a$ and
twice in $b$, and each traveler changes planes at most once.
:::

Each edge of the path separates $C_I$ from $C_G$, so the planes fly it towards $C_G$ at least
$t = 3$ times and back at least $t - p = 1$ time: $4 \cdot (1 + 2 + 1) = 16$ time units in total,
so one plane flies at least 8. In $f(U)$, every role configuration has four landings of cost 2,
and a $(B\bar B)$-pairing in either city puts a load of 10 on one plane. The plan above does in one
pattern what $f(U)$ cannot: leave a passenger at one vertex, fly to the next one, and take another
passenger there. This is the mechanism of the split crossings above. Giving $f(U)$ flights
between its cities does not repair the reduction either; its front then becomes
$\{(8, 10), (10, 8)\}$ (computed). On random small graphs, the two fronts differ on 342 of 4,000
paths, spokes, cycles and random graphs, and on none of 1,000 clique instances under (A1-NS).

The reduction is exact in three cases, and the general problem has an exact method of its own.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Proposition 6.15" >}} **Where the reduction is exact.**
$\mathcal F_U = \mathcal F_{f(U)}$ when $U$ is a clique instance satisfying (A1-NS), when $p = 1$,
and when $t = p$.
:::

Example 6.11 has $p = 2$ and $t = p + 1$, so the last two cases are sharp.
{{< node "Proposition 6.16" >}} shows that, with integer durations of at least 1, integer flows of
$p$ plane units and $t$ passenger units in the time-expanded network, passengers riding only where
a plane flies, give the least cost $R(M)$ of a plan of makespan at most $M$, and that
$\mathcal F_U = \{(R(M), M) : R(M) < R(M - 1)\}$: the exact front of a general instance is
computable, level by level, as an integer program.

**On the complexity:** In general the number of cities in $f(U)$ is not polynomial in function of
$n$, the number of cities in $U$, and thus, solving $U$ through $f(U)$ might be challenging w.r.t.
the initial complexity of the problem and our algorithm. On top of that, the number of paths
between two vertices can be up to super-exponential: a graph made of $\sqrt n$ layers of
$\sqrt n$ vertices has $(\sqrt n)^{\sqrt n}$ paths between its ends, and computing the cardinal of
the set of paths is already a $\sharp P$-complete problem [[Val79](index.qmd#ref-Val79)].

Not every path is needed. A path is *non-dominated* if no other path between the same vertices has
a landing cost and a duration both at most its own, one of them strictly smaller. Removing a city
of a clique instance without flights between central cities that another city dominates in cost,
$d$ and $\bar d$ does not change the front, so $f(U)$ keeps its front when built from the pairs of
non-dominated paths only ({{< node "Proposition 6.14" >}}). Some elements of the Pareto set, in the
decision space, may be lost, but the Pareto front of $f(U)$ is entirely found.

However, even in this case, the number of central cities in $f(U)$ is function of the cardinal of
the Pareto Set of non-dominated paths for each couple of cities in $U$. In
[[Han80](index.qmd#ref-Han80)], Hansen proposed some pathological instances of bicriterion graphs
such that the set of non-dominated paths between two extreme nodes is exponential in the number of
nodes $n$. Conversely, when the number of non-dominated paths of $U$ is bounded by a polynomial of
$n$, the number of cities of the reduced instance is polynomial of $n$.

In conclusion, the reduction of a general instance to a clique instance gives plans of the general
instance and its exact least cost, and its exact Pareto front when the instance is a clique under
(A1-NS), has one plane, or as many planes as passengers. In general, the exact front comes from
the integer flows of Proposition 6.16, on small instances; a characterization in the spirit of
Corollary 6.10 is open.
